section.heading: 5.9 Applications to Markov Chains
section.paragraph: The Markov chains described in this section are used as mathematical models of a wide variety of situations in biology, business, chemistry, engineering, physics, and elsewhere. In each case, the model is used to describe an experiment or measurement that is performed many times in the same way, where the outcome of each trial of the experiment will be one of several specified possible outcomes, and where the outcome of one trial depends only on the immediately preceding trial.
For example, if the population of a city and its suburbs were measured each year, then a vector such as
$$\textbf{x}_{0} = \begin{bmatrix} .60 \\ .40 \end{bmatrix}$$

could indicate that $$60\%$$ of the population lives in the city and $$40\%$$ in the suburbs. The decimals in $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ add up to $$1$$ because they account for the entire population of the region. Percentages are more convenient for our purposes here than population totals.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $$1$$ is called a probability vector. A stochastic matrix is a square matrix whose columns are probability vectors.

section.paragraph: A Markov chain is a sequence of probability vectors $$\textbf{x}_{0},\textbf{x}_{1},\textbf{x}_{2},\ldots$$ , together with a stochastic matrix $$P$$ , such that
$$\textbf{x}_{1} = P \textbf{x}_{0} , \textbf{x}_{2} = P \textbf{x}_{1} , \textbf{x}_{3} = P \textbf{x}_{2} , \ldots$$
Thus the Markov chain is described by the first-order difference equation
$$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = P \textbf{x}_{k} \text{for} k = 0 , 1 , 2 , \ldots$$

When a Markov chain of vectors in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ describes a system or a sequence of experiments, the entries in $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ list, respectively, the probabilities that the system is in each of $$n$$ possible states, or the probabilities that the outcome of the experiment is one of $$n$$ possible outcomes. For this reason, $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ is often called a state vector.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Section 1.10 examined a model for population movement between a city and its suburbs. See Figure 1. The annual migration between these two parts of the metropolitan region was governed by the migration matrix $$M$$ :

$$\begin{matrix}\begin{matrix} \text{From} \\ \text{City} \text{Suburbs} \text{To} \end{matrix} & \end{matrix} M = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.95 & .03 \\ .05 & .97\end{matrix} \left]\right. \begin{matrix} \text{City} \\ \text{Suburbs} \end{matrix}$$

That is, each year $$5\%$$ of the city population moves to the suburbs, and $$3\%$$ of the suburban population moves to the city. The columns of $$M$$ are probability vectors, so $$M$$ is a stochastic matrix. Suppose the 2020 population of the region is $$\text{600,000}$$ in the city and $$\text{400,000}$$ in the suburbs. Then the initial distribution of the population in the region is given previously by $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ in (1). What is the distribution of the population in 2021? In 2022?

image.alt: A figure shows two blocks labeled as city and suburbs with arrows showing annual percentage migration.

example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: In Example 3 of Section 1.10, we saw that after one year, the population vector $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 600,000 \\ 400,000 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ changed to
$$\begin{bmatrix} .95 & . 03 \\ .05 & . 97 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 600,000 \\ 400,000 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 582,000 \\ 418,000 \end{bmatrix}$$
If we divide both sides of this equation by the total population of $$1$$ million, and use the fact that $$kM\textbf{x} = M(k\textbf{x})$$ , we find that
$$\begin{bmatrix} .95 & . 03 \\ .05 & . 97 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} .600 \\ .400 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} .582 \\ .418 \end{bmatrix}$$

The vector $$\textbf{x}_{1} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} .582 \\ .418 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ gives the population distribution in 2021. That is, $$\text{58.2\%}$$ of the region lived in the city and $$\text{41.8\%}$$ lived in the suburbs. Similarly, the population distribution in 2022 is described by a vector $$\textbf{x}_{2}$$ , where
$$\textbf{x}_{2} = M \textbf{x}_{1} = \begin{bmatrix} .95 & . 03 \\ .05 & . 97 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} .582 \\ .418 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} .565 \\ .435 \end{bmatrix}$$

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Suppose the voting results of a congressional election at a certain voting precinct are represented by a vector $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ :
$$\textbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix} \% \text{voting} \text{Democratic} ( \text{D} ) \\ \% \text{voting} \text{Republican} ( \text{R} ) \\ \% \text{voting} \text{Other} ( \text{O} ) \end{bmatrix}$$

Suppose we record the outcome of the congressional election every two years by a vector of this type and the outcome of one election depends only on the results of the preceding election. Then the sequence of vectors that describe the votes every two years may be a Markov chain. As an example of a stochastic matrix $$P$$ for this chain, we take

$$\text{From} : \text{D} \text{R} \text{O} \text{To} : P = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.70 & .10 & .30 \\ .20 & .80 & .30 \\ .10 & .10 & .40\end{matrix} \left]\right. \begin{matrix} \text{D} \\ \text{R} \\ \text{O} \end{matrix}$$

The entries in the first column, labeled D, describe what the persons voting Democratic in one election will do in the next election. Here we have supposed that $$70\%$$ will vote D again in the next election, $$\text{20\%}$$ will vote R, and $$\text{10\%}$$ will vote O. Similar interpretations hold for the other columns of $$P$$ . A diagram for this matrix is shown in Figure 2.
example.heading: Figure 2
example.paragraph: Voting changes from one election to the next

image.alt: A block diagram consists of three blocks labeled democratic vote, republican vote, and other vote arranged in an inverted triangular structure with arrows in between that represent the distribution of voting changes.

figure.caption: Figure 1 Annual percentage migration between city and suburbs

example.paragraph: If the “transition” percentages remain constant over many years from one election to the next, then the sequence of vectors that give the voting outcomes forms a Markov chain. Suppose the outcome of one election is given by
$$\textbf{x}_{0} = \begin{bmatrix} .55 \\ .40 \\ .05 \end{bmatrix}$$
Determine the likely outcome of the next election and the likely outcome of the election after that.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The outcome of the next election is described by the state vector $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ and that of the election after that by $$\textbf{x}_{2}$$ , where

$$x_{1} = P x_{0} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.70 & .10 & .30 \\ .20 & .80 & .30 \\ .10 & .10 & .40\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.55 \\ .40 \\ .05\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.440 \\ .445 \\ .115\end{matrix} \left]\right. & \begin{matrix}44 \% \text{will} \text{vote} \text{D} . \\ 44.5 \% \text{will} \text{vote} \text{R} . \\ 11.5 \% \text{will} \text{vote} \text{O} .\end{matrix} & & & x_{2} = P x_{1} = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.70 & .10 & .30 \\ .20 & .80 & .30 \\ .10 & .10 & .40\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.440 \\ .445 \\ .115\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}.3870 \\ .4785 \\ .1345\end{matrix} \left]\right. & \begin{matrix}38.7 \% \text{will} \text{vote} \text{D} . \\ 47.9 \% \text{will} \text{vote} \text{R} . \\ 13.5 \% \text{will} \text{vote} \text{O} .\end{matrix}$$

To understand why $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ does indeed give the outcome of the next election, suppose $$1000$$ persons voted in the “first” election, with $$550$$ voting D, $$400$$ voting R, and $$50$$ voting O. (See the percentages in $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ .) In the next election, $$70\%$$ of the $$550$$ will vote D again, $$10\%$$ of the $$400$$ will switch from R to D, and $$30\%$$ of the $$50$$ will switch from O to D. Thus the total D vote will be
$$.70 \left(\right. 550 \left.\right) + .10 \left(\right. 400 \left.\right) + .30 \left(\right. 50 \left.\right) = 385 + 40 + 15 = 440$$

Thus $$44\%$$ of the vote next time will be for the D candidate. The calculation in (2) is essentially the same as that used to compute the first entry in $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ . Analogous calculations could be made for the other entries in $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ , for the entries in $$\textbf{x}_{2}$$ , and so on.

section.heading: Predicting the Distant Future
section.paragraph: The most interesting aspect of Markov chains is the study of a chain’s long-term behavior. For instance, what can be said in Example 2 about the voting after many elections have passed (assuming that the given stochastic matrix continues to describe the transition percentages from one election to the next)? Or, what happens to the population distribution in Example 1 “in the long run”? Here our work on eigenvalues and eigenvectors becomes helpful.

note.title: Theorem ﻿10﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿10﻿
Stochastic Matrices
note.paragraph: If $$P$$ is a stochastic matrix, then $$1$$ is an eigenvalue of $$P$$ .

section.heading: Proof﻿
section.paragraph: Since the columns of $$P$$ sum to $$1$$ , the rows of $$P^{T}$$ will also sum to $$1$$ . Let $$\textbf{e}$$ represent the vector for which every entry is $$1$$ . Notice that multiplying $$P^{T}$$ by $$\textbf{e}$$ has the effect of adding up the values in each row, hence $$P^{T}\textbf{e} = \textbf{e}$$ , establishing that $$\textbf{e}$$ is an eigenvector of $$P^{T}$$ with eigenvalue $$1$$ . Since $$P$$ and $$P^{T}$$ have the same eigenvalues (Exercise 20 in Section 5.2), $$1$$ is also an eigenvalue of $$P$$ .

In the next example, we see that the vectors generated in a Markov chain are almost the same as the vectors generated using the power method outlined in Section 5.8—the only difference is that in a Markov chain, the vectors are not scaled at each step. Based on our experience from Section 5.8, as $$k$$ increases we expect $$\textbf{x}_{k}\rightarrow\textbf{q}$$ , where $$\textbf{q}$$ is an eigenvector of $$P$$ .

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Let $$P = \begin{bmatrix} .5 & {.2} & {.3} \\ .3 & {.8} & {.3} \\ .2 & 0 & {.4} \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$\textbf{x}_{0} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Consider a system whose state is described by the Markov chain $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = P\textbf{x}_{k}$$ , for $$k = 0,1,\ldots$$ What happens to the system as time passes? Compute the state vectors $$\textbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{x}_{15}$$ to find out.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: $$\textbf{x}_{1 } & = P \textbf{x}_{0} & & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.5 & . 2 & . 3 \\ .3 & . 8 & . 3 \\ .2 & 0 & . 4\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.5 \\ .3 \\ .2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \textbf{x}_{2} & = P \textbf{x}_{1} & & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.5 & . 2 & . 3 \\ .3 & . 8 & . 3 \\ .2 & 0 & . 4\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.5 \\ .3 \\ .2\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.37 \\ .45 \\ .18\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \textbf{x}_{3} & = P \textbf{x}_{2} & & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.5 & . 2 & . 3 \\ .3 & . 8 & . 3 \\ .2 & 0 & . 4\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.37 \\ .45 \\ .18\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.329 \\ .525 \\ .146\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$
The results of further calculations are shown below, with entries rounded to four or five significant figures.

$$\textbf{x}_{4} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.3133 \\ .5625 \\ .1242\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , & \textbf{x}_{5} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.3064 \\ .5813 \\ .1123\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , & \textbf{x}_{6} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.3032 \\ .5906 \\ .1062\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , & \textbf{x}_{7} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.3016 \\ .5953 \\ .1031\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \textbf{x}_{8} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.3008 \\ .5977 \\ .1016\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , & \textbf{x}_{9} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.3004 \\ .5988 \\ .1008\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , & \textbf{x}_{10} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.3002 \\ .5994 \\ .1004\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , & \textbf{x}_{11} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.3001 \\ .5997 \\ .1002\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \textbf{x}_{12} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.30005 \\ .59985 \\ .10010\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , & \textbf{x}_{13} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.30002 \\ .59993 \\ .10005\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , & \textbf{x}_{14} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.30001 \\ .59996 \\ .10002\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} , & \textbf{x}_{15} & = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}.30001 \\ .59998 \\ .10001\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix}$$

These vectors seem to be approaching $$\textbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} .3 \\ .6 \\ .1 \end{bmatrix}$$ . The probabilities are hardly changing from one value of $$k$$ to the next. Observe that the following calculation is exact (with no rounding error):

$$P \textbf{q} = \left[\right. .5 & .2 & .3 .3 & .8 & .3 .2 & 0 & .4 \left]\right. \left[\right. .3 .6 .1 \left]\right. = \left[\right. .15 + .12 + .03 .09 + .48 + .03 .06 + 0 + .04 \left]\right. = \left[\right. .30 .60 .10 \left]\right. = \textbf{q}$$
When the system is in state $$\textbf{q}$$ , there is no change in the system from one measurement to the next.

section.heading: Steady-State Vectors
section.paragraph: If $$P$$ is a stochastic matrix, then a steady-state vector (or equilibrium vector) for $$P$$ is a probability vector $$\textbf{q}$$ such that
$$P \textbf{q} = \textbf{q}$$

In Theorem 10, it is established that $$1$$ is an eigenvalue of any stochastic matrix. It can be shown that $$1$$ is actually the largest eigenvalue of a stochastic matrix and the associated eigenvector can be chosen to be a steady-state vector. In Example 3, q is a steady-state vector for $$P$$ .

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: The probability vector $$\textbf{q} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} .375 \\ .625 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ is a steady-state vector for the population migration matrix $$M$$ in Example 1, because

$$M \textbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} .95 & .03 \\ .05 & .97 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} .375 \\ .625 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} .35625 + .01875 \\ .01875 + .60625 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} .375 \\ .625 \end{bmatrix} = \textbf{q}$$

section.paragraph: If the total population of the metropolitan region in Example 1 is $$1$$ million, then $$\textbf{q}$$ from Example 4 would correspond to having $$375,000$$ persons in the city and $$625,000$$ in the suburbs. At the end of one year, the migration out of the city would be $$(.05)(375,000) = 18,750$$ persons, and the migration into the city from the suburbs would be $$(.03)(625,000) = 18,750$$ persons. As a result, the population in the city would remain the same. Similarly, the suburban population would be stable.
The next example shows how to find a steady-state vector. Notice that we are just finding an eigenvector associated with the eigenvalue $$1$$ and then scaling it to create a probability vector.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Let $$P = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} .6 & .3 \\ .4 & .7 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Find a steady-state vector for $$P$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: First, solve the equation $$P\textbf{x} = \textbf{x}$$ .

$$P \textbf{x} - \textbf{x} & = \textbf{0} P \textbf{x} - I \textbf{x} & = \textbf{0} \text{Recall} \text{from} \text{Section} 1.4 \text{that} I \textbf{x} = \textbf{x} . \left(\right. P - I \left.\right) \textbf{x} & = \textbf{0}$$
For $$P$$ as above,
$$P - I = \begin{bmatrix} .6 & . 3 \\ .4 & . 7 \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} - .4 & .3 \\ .4 & - .3 \end{bmatrix}$$
To find all solutions of $$(P - I)\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ , row reduce the augmented matrix:
$$\begin{bmatrix} - .4 & . 3 & 0 \\ .4 & - .3 & 0 \end{bmatrix} sim \begin{bmatrix} - .4 & . 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 3 / 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$
Then $$x_{1} = \frac{3}{4}x_{2}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ is free. The general solution is $$x_{2}\begin{bmatrix} {3/4} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ .

Next, choose a simple basis for the solution space. One obvious choice is $$\begin{bmatrix} {3/4} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ but a better choice with no fractions is $$\textbf{w} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}$$ (corresponding to $$x_{2} = 4)$$ .

Finally, find a probability vector in the set of all solutions of $$P\textbf{x} = \textbf{x}$$ . This process is easy, since every solution is a multiple of the solution $$\textbf{w}$$ . Divide $$\textbf{w}$$ by the sum of its entries and obtain
$$\textbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 / 7 \\ 4 / 7 \end{bmatrix}$$
As a check, compute

$$P \textbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 / 10 & 3 / 10 \\ 4 / 10 & 7 / 10 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 / 7 \\ 4 / 7 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 18 / 70 + 12 / 70 \\ 12 / 70 + 28 / 70 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 30 / 70 \\ 40 / 70 \end{bmatrix} = \textbf{q}$$

section.paragraph: The next theorem shows that what happened in Example 3 is typical of many stochastic matrices. We say that a stochastic matrix is regular if some matrix power $$P^{k}$$ contains only strictly positive entries. For $$P$$ in Example 3,
Since every entry in $$P^{2}$$ is strictly positive, $$P$$ is a regular stochastic matrix.

Also, we say that a sequence of vectors, $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ for $$k = 1 , 2 , \ldots ,$$ converges to a vector $$\textbf{q}$$ as $$k\rightarrow \text{∞}$$ , if the entries in $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ can be made as close as desired to the corresponding entries in $$\textbf{q}$$ by taking $$k$$ sufficiently large.

note.title: ﻿﻿﻿Theorem ﻿11﻿
note.heading: ﻿﻿﻿Theorem ﻿11﻿
note.paragraph: If $$P$$ is an $$n \times n$$ regular stochastic matrix, then $$P$$ has a unique steady-state vector $$\textbf{q}$$ . Further, if $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ is any initial state and $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = P\textbf{x}_{k}$$ for $$k = 0,1,2,\ldots,$$ then the Markov chain $$\{\textbf{x}_{k}\}$$ converges to $$\textbf{q}$$ as $$k\rightarrow \text{∞}$$ .

section.paragraph: This theorem is proved in standard texts on Markov chains. The amazing part of the theorem is that the initial state has no effect on the long-term behavior of the Markov chain.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: In Example 2, what percentage of the voters are likely to vote for the Republican candidate in some election many years from now, assuming that the election outcomes form a Markov chain?
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: If you want to compute the precise entries of the steady-state vector by hand, it is better to recognize that it is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $$1$$ rather than to pick some initial vector $$\textbf{x}_{0}$$ and compute $$\textbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{x}_{k}$$ for some large value of $$k$$ . You have no way of knowing how many vectors to compute, and you cannot be sure of the limiting values of the entries in $$\textbf{x}_{k}$$ .

A better approach is to compute the steady-state vector and then appeal to Theorem 11. Given $$P$$ as in Example 2, form $$P - I$$ by subtracting $$1$$ from each diagonal entry in $$P$$ . Then row reduce the augmented matrix:
$$\begin{bmatrix} \left(\right. P - I \left.\right) & \textbf{0} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} - .3 & . 1 & . 3 & 0 \\ .2 & - . 2 & . 3 & 0 \\ .1 & . 1 & - . 6 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$$
Recall from earlier work with decimals that the arithmetic is simplified by multiplying each row by $$10$$ .1

The general solution of $$(P - I)\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$$ is $$x_{1} = \frac{9}{4}x_{3},x_{2} = \frac{15}{4}x_{3}$$ , and $$x_{3}$$ is free. Choosing $$x_{3} = 4$$ , we obtain a basis for the solution space whose entries are integers, and from this we easily find the steady-state vector whose entries sum to $$1$$ :
$$\textbf{w} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ 15 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} , \text{and} \textbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} 9 / 28 \\ 15 / 28 \\ 4 / 28 \end{bmatrix} \approx \begin{bmatrix} .32 \\ .54 \\ .14 \end{bmatrix}$$

The entries in $$\textbf{q}$$ describe the distribution of votes at an election to be held many years from now (assuming the stochastic matrix continues to describe the changes from one election to the next). Thus, eventually, about $$54\%$$ of the vote will be for the Republican candidate.

note.title: Numerical Notes﻿
note.heading: Numerical Notes﻿
note.paragraph: You may have noticed that if $$\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = P\textbf{x}_{k}$$ for $$k = 0,1,\ldots,$$ then

To compute a specific vector such as $$\textbf{x}_{3}$$ , fewer arithmetic operations are needed to compute $$\textbf{x}_{1},\textbf{x}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{x}_{3}$$ , rather than $$P^{3}$$ and $$P^{3}\textbf{x}_{0}$$ . However, if $$P$$ is small—say, $$30 \times 30$$ —the machine computation time is insignificant for both methods, and a command to compute $$P^{3}\textbf{x}_{0}$$ might be preferred because it requires fewer human keystrokes.
